title: "Computational Scalability of Deterministic and Two-Stage Stochastic MILP Models for Grain-Storage Network Design and Hub Location"
date: 2026-10-30
abstract: >-
  Designing grain-storage networks requires decisions about facility location,
  storage capacity and grain handling before uncertain supply and demand are
  known. The resulting mixed-integer linear programs can contain millions of
  operating decisions, making computational requirements central to their use
  in agricultural planning. This study evaluates deterministic and two-stage
  stochastic models through model dimensions, construction and optimization
  time, memory use and independently checked solution quality. Warehouse-only
  instances contain 215 to 500 facilities, with nine supply–demand scenarios
  in the stochastic model. The stochastic formulation grows from 14.1 to
  63.4 million variables across this range. All nine warehouse-only Gurobi
  observations satisfy the prescribed 1% relative-gap criterion; the
  500-facility instance reaches a 0.21% gap in approximately 128 minutes of
  native optimization. The returned stochastic plans allocate capacity
  investment across the admitted candidate sites, indicating distributed
  capacity sizing within the available network. Substantial handling and
  storage exceedances and unmet demand remain in the penalized solutions.
  The assessment therefore connects attainable computational scale to the
  physical meaning of the investment and operating decisions. Evaluating
  solution quality together with service, stock and throughput reveals
  which conclusions the optimized plans support for grain-storage planning.

# Introduction

Grain-storage networks connect seasonal harvests with demand distributed across
places and periods. Choosing where to open or expand warehouses affects how
much grain can be held, how quickly it can be received and dispatched, and
which markets the network can serve.

Brazil's Artificial Intelligence Plan for 2024–2028 identifies high-performance computing infrastructure and technical capacity as priorities for research and innovation ([MCTI, 2025](https://www.gov.br/mcti/pt-br/acompanhe-o-mcti/transformacaodigital/plano-brasileiro-de-inteligencia-artificial-pbia-_vf.pdf)). The National Laboratory for Scientific Computing is developing a separate AI-oriented supercomputing installation in Macaíba, Rio Grande do Norte ([LNCC, 2026](https://www.gov.br/lncc/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/ultimas-noticias-1/lncc-conduz-implantacao-de-supercomputador-de-inteligencia-artificial-que-ampliara-a-capacidade-computacional-do-brasil)). Agricultural research has related infrastructure needs. Embrapa's AgroDigital initiative has acquired high-performance computing and GPU servers to support research that requires substantial data processing and storage ([Embrapa Agricultura Digital, 2024](https://www.embrapa.br/en/busca-de-noticias/-/noticia/93647060/recursos-do-novo-pac-sao-aplicados-na-modernizacao-do-data-center-para-pdi-da-embrapa)). These initiatives illustrate the importance of computing infrastructure across research domains.

Grain-storage planning raises a specific computational problem. The selection of warehouse sites and the sizing of storage and handling capacity combine discrete investment choices with flows that vary across products, periods and scenarios. A larger network increases the number of decisions and can place substantial demands on model construction, memory and solution time. This study uses experiments at NPAD/UFRN to examine the conditions under which deterministic and two-stage stochastic mixed-integer linear programs yield independently checked, interpretable plans for soybean and corn storage networks. The analysis relates measured computational requirements and attainable solution quality to the investment and operating decisions that the models return.

Grain-storage location and integrated network design are established research
topics [@essien2018; @gholamian2017]. Agricultural network uncertainty has also
been addressed through wheat-network design and tactical soybean planning
[@hosseini2020; @reis2023]. Decomposition and distributed computing already
provide computational precedents in agricultural MILP [@shastri2011].
The study connects the effort needed to construct and solve these models with
the certified quality and agricultural implications of the plans they return.

The central question is: **How computational scalability affects the optimal
resolution of grain-storage network design and hub location models?** Here
*optimal resolution* concerns the quality attainable when solving the MILP.
It includes exact optimality, feasible incumbents with certified gaps,
resource-censored results and no-incumbent outcomes; it does not presume that
every optimization proves an exact optimum.

The general objective is to investigate the effects of computational scalability
in the resolution of grain-storage network design and hub location models.

support.

| SO3 Agricultural interpretation | Interpret validated location, capacity-investment and grain-distribution decisions across h215, h300, h400 and h500 when accepted outputs are available | C2 |

: Research objectives. {#tbl-objectives}

The contributions have three distinct roles. C1 characterizes observed matrix
dimensions, construction and solution effort, memory and certified gaps across
the evaluated populations. C2 interprets the returned investment and operating
decisions by separating financial costs, artificial penalties, domestic service
and capacity exceedances. C3 documents human-supervised AI assistance and
verification as a complementary account of research practice, detailed in
Appendix B.

The next section situates these contributions in agricultural planning and
computational optimization. The methods and results then connect the model,
resource measurements and independently checked solutions to storage-network
decisions.

# Related work and research positioning

## Grain-storage planning as an integrated decision problem

The systematic review by @rosa2025 places grain-warehouse location within a
broader family of mathematical planning models. Complementarily, @garima2024
organize grain supply-chain decision research around operational complexity,
risk, infrastructure, stakeholders and solution methods. Together, these
perspectives show why adding sites to a location model is insufficient: a
strategic design must connect storage, seasonal handling and access to markets.
The following synthesis compares published approaches along these substantive
dimensions. [Appendix A](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/supplementary-review.html)
provides the search strategy, selection record and
the complete researcher-supplied literature review.

Comparisons based on abstracts or publisher previews are limited to the
methods and results reported there. Appendix B records the scope of the
source review.

Integrated wheat-network design in @gholamian2017 links infrastructure choices
to the organization of the supply chain. Scenario-based wheat planning in
@pourmohammadi2020 and sustainable, resilient network design in
@hosseini2020 extend this perspective to uncertain conditions and competing
performance concerns. These contributions motivate an integrated treatment,
but their commodity systems, constraints and objectives cannot be transferred
unchanged to a Brazilian grain-storage network. In particular, resilience to
disruption, seasonal variation and a numerical relaxation of capacity are
different concepts. A slack preserves a mathematical solution; it does not by
itself provide the transport, temporary equipment or institutional arrangements
that would make the physical network resilient.

@essien2018 address stakeholder objectives in grain-storage planning, and
@filippi2022 examine the governance of rural warehouse condominiums. In the
goal-programming model of @essien2018, the number of sites is prescribed and
stakeholder transport targets enter the objective. Here the model sizes
capacity and links investment to scenario-dependent operation. Land access,
financing and operating agreements remain part of the appraisal of any
candidate location.

## Closest precedents and the scope of the empirical question

The closest agricultural studies establish why location and uncertainty alone
cannot define this article's gap. @tbl-closest-precedents distinguishes their
decision or computational emphasis from the assessment undertaken here.
The studies differ in decision horizon, infrastructure choices and solution
method. These distinctions determine which aspects can inform the present
assessment.

| Precedent | Established decision or computational emphasis | Question examined here |
|:--|:--|:--|
| @essien2018 | Multi-stakeholder grain-storage location and decision support | How do returned investment and service outcomes relate to a certified scalar objective? |
| @gholamian2017 | Integrated wheat-network planning, including silo location and distribution | What construction, solution and memory requirements accompany explicitly defined extensive-form instances? |
| @pourmohammadi2020 | Scenario-based location and discrete storage sizing with hard demand fulfillment | How do continuous capacity sizing and penalized shortages change the interpretation of returned plans? |
| @hosseini2020 | Wheat-network design/redesign with sustainability and resilience concerns | What do the present cost and slack variables support, without adding unmodeled resilience or sustainability outcomes? |
| @reis2023 | Two-stage tactical soybean LP with purchasing and transport contracts; 243 scenarios | How does shared infrastructure investment differ from tactical contracting under uncertainty? |
| @shastri2011 | Decomposition and distributed solution of an agricultural MILP | What attainable quality and resource use are observed for the present direct extensive-form solution? |

: Closest agricultural and computational precedents. Models, data, hardware and
stopping criteria differ; the rows are not matched runtime comparisons. {#tbl-closest-precedents}

@reis2023 provide a computational precedent for tactical soybean planning.
Their model concerns purchasing and transport contracts within a given network.
The tactical stochastic LP contains 1,987,225 variables and
2,288,220 constraints across 243 scenarios. Section 6.1 and Table 8 compare
barrier, dual simplex and primal simplex with CPLEX 20.1, reporting solution
times of 84.61, 246.9 and 328.91 seconds and peak-memory figures of 2720,
2131 and 1902, respectively, in the table's stated unit of Mb. Thus, both
algorithm comparison and memory measurement already have an agricultural
planning precedent. Their first-stage decisions concern grain purchasing and
transport contracts; recourse includes spot-market purchases, processing,
sales and physical flows. The present investment MILP asks a different
planning question and adds explicit attention to construction, attained
integer-solution quality and the physical interpretation of the returned
capacity plan. Different formulations, hardware and measurement definitions
preclude interpreting the published times or memory figures as matched
performance baselines.

These studies motivate distinct comparisons. Discrete sizing and hard demand
fulfillment in @pourmohammadi2020 clarify how continuous capacity choices
and penalized shortage affect the interpretation of a returned plan.
@hosseini2020 treat sustainability and resilience as modeled concerns,
whereas the present study reports service and exceedances under its stated
constraints. @shastri2011 evaluate decomposition and distributed solution.
The present experiments characterize construction effort, attained quality
and resource use for a direct extensive-form solution and connect the
resulting decisions to grain-storage operations.

## Network representation and decision horizons

Dynamic-network models connect storage investment to grain flows over time
[@foulds2005]. In a Brazilian soybean setting, @mascarenhas2014 study
warehousing location with road and intermodal export connections. The
distinction is consequential: a throughput facility that transfers arrivals
onward is not interchangeable with a warehouse that carries inventory between
months. Static stock capacity, annual throughput and vehicle capacity must
therefore remain separate dimensions in a benchmark.

The logistics-integration-center formulation of @guimaraes2017 preserves
origin-destination demand relationships. By contrast, the present model
conserves each product but does not retain an origin label after it enters a
warehouse. Product from different origins can satisfy the same customer's
demand. This assumption is appropriate for a fungible-commodity planning
abstraction, but not for tracing contracts, quality lots or individual consignments.
It is a substantive difference in the feasible set, not simply a change of indices.

Terminal siting in @morais2023 connects location, capacity choices and
access to railways or waterways. @milanez2026 integrate soybean export
network design with hub functions and economies of scale. One variant permits seaport-capacity overflow at a penalty, and Table 2
reports CPU time and CPLEX gaps. Penalized capacity relief and computational
quality reporting therefore have direct precedents. These studies motivate reporting storage and transport decisions together.
The present network represents road movements to domestic destinations and
export ports. Multimodal models also represent modal transfers and transport
beyond those outlets.

@tbl-literature summarizes the selected studies and the modeling distinctions
that determine whether their results are comparable.

| Study | Network and decision emphasis | Comparison implication |
|:--|:--|:--|
| @foulds2005 | Dynamic grain-silo location and flow | Separate network size, capacity decisions and temporal flow |
| @mascarenhas2014 | Mato Grosso soybean warehouses and export connections | Distinguish throughput facilities from stock-carrying warehouses |
| @guimaraes2017 | Logistics integration centers and peer-to-peer demand | Commodity mixing differs from origin-destination preservation |
| @morais2023 | Capacitated terminals with intermodal location preferences | Modal access is not equivalent to a road-distance proxy |
| @milanez2026 | Hub location and soybean-export network design | Report hub function, capacity and route use together |
| @granillo2019 | Contract-farming network with simulation and MILP | Simulation-based uncertainty is not automatically two-stage recourse |
| @mendoza2021 | Scenario-based agro-food facility location | State which decisions precede the uncertain outcome |
| @vazquez2021 | Guayule/guar supply-chain design with sustainability criteria | Processing yields and sustainability constraints change comparability |
| @mogale2020 | Multi-echelon grain network with risk and losses | Losses and discrete transport resources require additional balances |

: Selected agricultural network-design studies and their implications for
comparability. The studies address different commodities and decision scopes. {#tbl-literature}

## Parameters, decisions and objective functions

Economic formulations typically connect fixed facility choices to continuous
material flows. The opening variable controls whether infrastructure can be
used, while installed capacity determines how much can be stored or handled.
A benchmark must distinguish a fixed-size site choice from scalable capacity:
both may contain a binary opening variable, but their investment feasible
sets differ. Counting producing regions or candidate sites is not an integer
decision variable unless the optimizer actually selects that count.

Agricultural models also differ in the economic boundary. Freight and
construction alone do not represent the same objective as freight, inventory,
processing, emissions, losses and employment. @mogale2020 include risk and
post-harvest losses in a green food supply-chain design. @vazquez2021 connect
supply-chain design to environmental and social impacts; @mogale2023 examine
social sustainability. Those dimensions are relevant to public planning but
are outside the scope of the present formulation. We report neither avoided
emissions nor jobs created from a reduction in transport distance alone.

The cost evidence available to the present study is strongest at the
capacity-unit level. Introducing an arbitrary fixed construction charge on
top of a whole-project cost per tonne would risk counting part of the project
twice. Conversely, registry placeholders equal to zero do not establish that
investment is free. The data translation must state whether a quoted total
cost is represented by a fixed term, a capacity-proportional term, or a
documented decomposition. Sensitivity to uncertain investment costs is a
future economic analysis, not something to conceal through a large shortage
penalty.

Brazilian logistics costs also depend on more than distance. @kussano2012
analyze soybean export logistics using a broader cost accounting boundary,
including factors that can alter the ranking of modal alternatives. Accordingly,
The road-network distances enter a freight approximation based on modeled
loads and unit transport costs. Congestion, taxes, service contracts
and seasonally changing tariffs remain possible sources of divergence between
the least-cost modeled route and actual grain movements.

Spatial suitability and network optimization are complementary rather than
substitutable. @souza2024 use spatial multicriteria analysis for agricultural
warehouse location; such screening can constrain the candidate set before a
flow model allocates capacity. The present candidate population preserves
geographic and facility-type diversity but does not replace environmental,
land-use or engineering suitability assessment. Similarly, the wider
agricultural and carbon implications of Brazilian transport infrastructure
examined by @wang2024 lie outside a freight-and-storage objective. A shorter
modeled route cannot be interpreted automatically as a net environmental gain.

## Uncertainty and strategic interpretation

Uncertainty can enter a model through simulation, scenarios, robust
constraints or probabilistic objectives. These approaches answer different
questions. @granillo2019 combine a deterministic optimization model with
simulation in a barley contract-farming network. @mendoza2021 study
scenario-based facility location, while the adoption scenarios in
@vazquez2021 concern a different source of uncertainty. They should not be
classified as interchangeable simply because each uses multiple scenarios.

@pourmohammadi2020 provide a closer stochastic infrastructure precedent:
six equiprobable supply-demand scenarios, shared choices among four
facility-capacity levels, and scenario-dependent operation. Their
assumptions prohibit shortage and include imports, quality blending and
road/rail transport. The present instance instead sizes capacity
continuously, represents road movements and permits penalized shortages.
These differences change the feasible set and the meaning of cost and
service outcomes.

@maiyar2019 model emergency hubs as physical options for disruptions. The
slacks used in the present study quantify excess demand on nominal capacity
within the modeled network.

Integrated decision support links planning horizons rather than treating
optimization in isolation [@mardaneh2021]. The joint crop-establishment,
harvesting and network-design perspective of @anselmino2025 provides another
example, in bioenergy rather than grain storage. Such work motivates clear
interfaces between data preparation, strategic investment and operational
evaluation. It does not imply that harvest scheduling or crop establishment
has been implemented in this demonstrator.

## Computational approaches in agricultural systems

@shastri2011 address a large agricultural optimization model through a
decomposition and distributed-computing approach to BioFeed, a biomass supply
planning problem. This is direct precedent for treating computational solution
strategy, rather than the use of a commercial optimizer alone, as a research
contribution. Our current extensive-form implementation does not reproduce
their decomposition or establish superiority over it.

@knapen2025 use standard big-data and distributed-computing technologies for
scalable crop-growth simulations. Their application illustrates a different
parallelization opportunity: distributing simulation work is not equivalent to
solving a MILP whose scenarios share first-stage integer decisions. @zhao2012
study parallelization and optimization of spatial analysis for environmental
model-data assembly. This distinction supports measuring data preparation
separately from the numerical solver rather than attributing all elapsed time
to optimization.

Shared-memory performance also requires explicit measurement. The PaScal Suite
of @silva2025pascal provides tools for evaluating and profiling parallel
scalability. Work on parallel dual revised simplex by @huangfu2018 shows that
parallelism may be organized within and across iterations. These references
motivate region-level timings and controlled thread-count experiments; they
do not imply that PaScal is integrated here or identify Gurobi's proprietary
internal algorithms.

@tbl-computational-literature relates the agricultural planning problem to
computational approaches at the optimization, simulation and data-processing
levels.

| Computational layer | Published precedent | Present implementation and evidence boundary |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Agricultural MILP solution strategy | @shastri2011 | Direct extensive-form solution; decomposition is not implemented in the evaluated scalar pipeline |
| Distributed agricultural simulation | @knapen2025 | Slurm experiment scheduling, not a distributed scenario solver |
| Spatial data preparation | @zhao2012 | Versioned OSRM materialization and pair-cache reuse; no matched speedup benchmark |
| Shared-memory profiling | @silva2025pascal | Separate workflow timings; descriptive single-observation thread contrast, not a controlled scaling estimate |
| LP parallel algorithms | @huangfu2018 | Solver method and thread settings recorded, without claims about proprietary internals |

: Computational precedents and the boundaries of the present contribution.
These studies address different workloads and are not runtime baselines for
the present instances. {#tbl-computational-literature}


# Materials and methods

The investment formulation follows @rosa2026thesis in its treatment of
facility opening, expansion and bulk-handling conversion. The scalar
objective charges investments once and weights recourse costs by scenario
probability. Investment decisions are shared across scenarios, and each
scenario has a separate operating trajectory [@birge2011].

{{< include formulation.qmd >}}

## Data lineage and network construction

Input workbooks, materialization audits, exact included warehouse IDs and
selection records are frozen with each attempt. The populations contain
146 existing facilities and respectively 69, 154, 254 and 354
candidate sites at h215, h300, h400 and h500. The canonical 69 candidate anchors
are retained; additional candidates follow the original deterministic,
proportionally stratified order across state, warehouse type and static-capacity
quartile. The selection seed and source/anchor/ranking hashes are preserved.
Included candidates are investment options, not decisions made by the optimizer.

The processed input workbooks contain 37 distinct supply-location identifiers
for soybean and corn, 27 domestic-capital destinations and ten export-destination
roles. A city may have both domestic and export roles. The counts refer to input entities and their respective roles.
Coordinates are retained exactly and coincident identifiers remain distinct.
The accepted exported solutions use nine export destinations with positive
transport. This does not redefine the ten available export options.

Road distances come from the frozen Brazilian OpenStreetMap extract
`brazil-260901`. The recorded NPAD materialization workflow uses OSRM 6.0.0
in Singularity with a driving profile and the multilevel Dijkstra algorithm.
OSRM's Table API supplies directed lengths in metres along the configured
fastest routes. The pair cache reuses distances for the same dataset,
profile and ordered coordinates, and the frozen workbooks retain distances
in kilometres. Appendix D gives the dataset and container identities and
identifies the audited cache and workbook inputs.

The h215, h300, h400 and h500 workbooks record 63,289, 113,269, 190,569 and
287,869 directed road pairs, all from OSRM. The MILP selects a subset of
product-eligible arcs and retains eligible pairs for connectivity repairs.
A larger population can change the screened graph even when the warehouse
memberships are nested.

DET uses the original deterministic arrays. STO combines three supply and three
demand multiplier levels into nine Cartesian scenarios of probability 1/9.
These are controlled experimental scenarios, not fitted event frequencies or
a forecast validation. The low/base/high supply factors are 0.85/1/1.15 and
the domestic-demand factors are 0.95/1/1.05, read from the frozen workbook.
Every supply level is crossed with every demand level; the nine combinations
each receive probability 1/9. The models have two products and 60 ordered planning
periods. All warehouse-only scalability cases disable direct origin-to-customer
arcs; the separate h215 D comparison enables them. Optional memory compaction
is disabled in both cohorts. The objective is an undiscounted BRL total
over the declared horizon. No verified common price year, inflation adjustment,
currency conversion or discount rate is introduced.

## Experimental and validation protocol

Each run starts from a frozen workbook and ordered warehouse population.
The input stage derives the effective costs, scenario trajectories and
product-specific network. The builder constructs the MILP for the declared
solver and stopping settings. After solution, the workflow exports decisions
and records phase times and memory. Independent checks reconstruct balances
and costs in their original units. The solution and bound then support the
interpretation of service, stock and throughput. Appendix C details the
common Pyomo implementation.

The warehouse-only scalar cohort comprises nine accepted observations: h215
DET/STO, the h300 thread sequence 4, 1, 8, 2, 16, and h400/h500 STO with one
thread each. The separate h215 D DET/STO observations bring the scalar inventory
to eleven; they are not eleven independent replications. Each uses a global
native TimeLimit of 14,400 seconds, MIPGap 0.01, Seed 42 and penalties of
90000 BRL/t for domestic shortage and 45000 BRL/t for each of the two
capacity-exceedance terms, with their period units defined in Appendix D. The h215 pair uses four solver threads.
The h300 levels are cold serial observations in one reservation, without
replication or randomized order. The one-thread h400 and h500 configurations were selected using the
descriptive h300 observations; that selection does not establish a generally
optimal thread count. Here cold means a fresh native model without an incumbent warm
start; operating-system caches and shared-node load were not controlled.
Original decisions, bounds and independent validation records were retained
for each observation. Subsequent integrity checks verify those records without
constituting new optimization runs.

Software qualification precedes experimental acceptance. Analytical examples
check objective reconstruction, investment charged once, deterministic/singleton
equivalence, probability weighting, slack units, connectivity and activation.
Licensed miniature tests establish implementation behavior at their tested scope;
they are not large-instance results. Experiments use fixed source versions and declared resource limits.
The research records retain partial and failed attempts as well as successful
calculations.

Independent original-unit validation reconstructs objective components and
checks the exported decisions against the encoded constraints, retaining
absolute 1e-5 and relative 1e-8 tolerances. An original accepted certificate
is distinct from a later portable integrity replay. The latter verifies
retained evidence and arithmetic; a fresh reproduction must validate newly
exported decisions against its input. Scheduler completion, incumbent existence, model feasibility and
attainment of the scalar quality criterion are reported separately.
Failure to find an incumbent within a resource budget is not a proof of
mathematical infeasibility. A time- or memory-censored result does not
demonstrate a speedup over another censored result.
For minimization, the common relative gap is $(z-b)/|z|$ for finite nonzero
incumbent $z$ and bound $b\le z$. Both zero imply gap zero; missing/nonfinite
values or inconsistent bounds are not assigned a finite accepted gap.
Native solver conventions are retained separately.

The additional Pyomo implementation separates the algebraic model from the
optimizer. The same scalar formulation is transferred through Pyomo's APPSI
interfaces to Gurobi, using gurobipy, or to HiGHS, using highspy.
Public analytical and Excel-to-validation controls check the adapters against
the same physical constraints and cost reconstruction. These tests establish
implementation behavior; they do not constitute additional large-instance
performance observations.

Candidate slack indicators use a disclosed bounded representative formulation.
With nonnegative slack costs, trimming redundant excess preserves the
physical/investment projection and optimal scalar value. The derived bounds
follow cumulative stock conservation and hard shipping capacity, including
transshipment circulation (Appendix C). This equivalence does not imply
identical native relaxations or search paths. The independently validated
h215 HiGHS result is reported separately from software qualification and the
Gurobi scaling sequence.

The modeling interface does not select a common search strategy or initial
solution for the solvers. Algorithmic defaults are distinguished from explicit
time, gap, thread, seed and numerical-tolerance settings in each experiment
record. In particular, the documented seed value 42 controls solver-specific
pseudorandom choices; it does not supply the same starting incumbent across
different optimizers.

Parallelism is version specific. In HiGHS 1.15.1, the thread setting limits
available workers, while `parallel="on"` enables parallel branch-and-bound
exploration. It does not make every phase parallel: the release disables
parallel simplex for the LP relaxations within MIP. Consequently, root-LP
work can limit gains from additional threads. The retained h215 HiGHS
observation used four threads with parallel tree search disabled; it remains
distinct from the prospective parallel-search campaign. Appendix C explains
these settings and their interpretation using the
[versioned parallelism documentation](https://github.com/ERGO-Code/HiGHS/blob/v1.15.1/docs/src/parallel.md)
and [release notes](https://github.com/ERGO-Code/HiGHS/releases/tag/v1.15.1).

### Common-Pyomo comparison campaign

The campaign uses the common Pyomo builder with Gurobi and HiGHS on the
frozen h300, h400 and h500 W STO instances. Two solvers, three populations,
five thread ceilings (1, 2, 4, 8 and 16) and three temporal repetitions give
90 planned runs. Each run has an eight-hour native allowance, a 1% gap
target and seed 42. This HiGHS profile enables parallel tree search.
An independent process starts each run. Thread settings can change search
trajectories even with a fixed seed. The repetitions describe execution
variability on the same instance and seed. The historical observations form
separate cohorts.

The first one-thread h300 pair has audited evidence. The 16-thread pilots
also have collector receipts, and Appendix C distinguishes them from the
later preliminary terminal records. Progression across populations follows
the existing resource and validation criteria.

## HPC experimental environment

The experiments use NPAD/UFRN's Intel shared-memory infrastructure under Slurm
[@npad2026]. Retained runtime receipts identify Intel Xeon E5-2698 v3 CPUs,
Python 3.13 and Gurobi 13.0.3. The scalar allocations request 24 logical CPUs
and 192 GiB. Gurobi's SoftMemLimit is 160 decimal GB; it is not a process-RSS
ceiling. The historical native h300 worker affinity pool contains 16 logical CPU IDs across
12 physical cores, including SMT siblings. It does not represent disabled
hyperthreading or sixteen physical cores. Solver threads, affinity and allocated
logical CPUs are distinct resource scopes.

For the common-Pyomo campaign the profile requests an exclusive node and
192 GiB for a 12-hour allocation. The h300 worker affinity is 16 logical
CPU IDs. Active roots in the partial scheduler record show 64 allocated
logical CPUs for those jobs. Solver thread ceilings are settings within
this envelope. The runtime and hardware receipts identify the conditions
for each numerical observation.

Historical native reservations are 14 hours for the h215 pair, 30 hours for the five-arm h300
block, and eight hours each for h400 and h500. Reservation time is not measured
optimizer time. Current models solve within one allocated node, and the
reported scalar blocks run serially. Distributing independent experiments
through scheduler arrays would not make an individual model a distributed MILP
solve; no multi-node speedup is claimed. Network preparation, construction
and post-processing are CPU workloads outside the primary optimization call.
No GPU acceleration or use of the InfiniBand fabric by a distributed MILP
algorithm is asserted.

## Model size, memory and performance measurement

With retained product-eligible arcs $\mathcal A_p$, flow variables grow as
$|S||T|\sum_p|\mathcal A_p|$. Inventory contributes terms proportional to
$|S||T||W||P|$, with separate slack and first-stage blocks. Before screening,
the directed interwarehouse graph can contain $|W|(|W|-1)$ arcs. A fixed retained
fraction therefore does not eliminate quadratic network growth. These are
structural matrix counts, not an asymptotic algorithmic-complexity proof.

Native Runtime, model-construction wall time, application optimization wall
time, extraction, validation, export and application end-to-end time are
separate clocks. Allocation elapsed includes additional staging and control.
The microsecond data-read fields at an already-loaded model layer are not
large-workbook ETL timings. We do not reconstruct missing phases by subtracting
overlapping clocks. Memory labels distinguish sampled application RSS,
solver-managed memory and Slurm step MaxRSS. Sampling may miss an instantaneous
peak; requested memory and allocated CPU-hour products are not measured
consumption or billing.

For a fixed instance and solver, strong scaling varies resources while
holding the problem fixed. With comparable work, timing and quality
criteria, speedup is $S(p)=T(1)/T(p)$ and parallel efficiency is
$E(p)=S(p)/p$ for a $p$-fold resource setting relative to the baseline.
In this study a ratio normalized by the configured thread ceiling measures
performance relative to that setting. Effective CPU utilization requires
a separate measurement. A time-to-target comparison uses the recorded time
when a common quality threshold is first attained. Terminal runtime also
includes work up to the observed stopping condition.

Across populations the experiment evaluates problem-size and resource
scaling. The selected graph and the number of nonzeros change
nonproportionally, while classical weak scaling keeps the workload per
resource approximately constant. Nonzeros per thread describe structural
load. Solver parallelism concerns work within one solve. Concurrent Slurm
jobs concern independent executions. Throughput would count specified
completed work per unit elapsed time over a stated allocation and
observation window.

## Geographic interpretation and figure preparation

A separate persistent geographic SQLite binds entity identities, coordinates,
nested memberships, accepted decision records and available OSRM road geometry
to source hashes. Preparation is explicit; local Plotly Dash callbacks and
Linux headless PDF/PNG/SVG rendering open it read-only. Content-derived snapshot
keys reuse unchanged data. Neither viewing nor rendering invokes an optimizer,
requests routes or changes the experimental distance cache.

The Dash and static renderers share scientific figure definitions, filters,
node styles and legends. The static Python renderer uses no browser, GUI,
Dash server or Kaleido. Official IBGE 2023 national and federative-unit vectors
provide a neutral geographic background. The source SIRGAS 2000 geometries are
transformed to WGS84 after a topology-preserving simplification; both renderers
apply the same Albers equal-area display and fixed national extent. Original
facility coordinates are retained. The cached background is independent of
facility selection and the road-distance data. Map lines delineate study
areas and do not necessarily depict accepted national boundaries.
Existing/candidate availability, candidate activation,
positive capacity investment and use by transport/inventory are distinct.
Product, period and scenario filters are explicit; aggregation across scenarios
uses the original probabilities.

The supplied road-distance workbooks do not contain route polylines.
Accordingly, the prepared scientific maps show verified node and investment
locations; positive-flow route geometry is unavailable and is not replaced by
straight segments. The software accepts separately source-bound OSRM geometry
for positive routes when it becomes available. Transport incidence and
quantities remain analyzable from the original vectors without inventing a
physical road path. The h500 investment map is reconstructed from its original
accepted decision CSV and source-bound facility coordinates. Its original
input-availability map remains separately retained. This investment-only
reconstruction does not establish facility use or recover original flow geometry.

# Discussion

## Computational scale and attainable solution quality

Each accepted scalar observation pairs an independently validated feasible
incumbent with a finite bound and an attained relative gap within the
prescribed 1% tolerance. The reported gap quantifies the remaining
uncertainty in the penalized objective at termination.

The h300 one-thread, h400 and h500 observations connect increasing matrix dimensions
to higher observed construction time, optimizer time and memory. The expanded
warehouse set also changes retained routes and available investment choices.
Consequently, these observations cannot isolate population size as the sole
cause of runtime or objective changes. Larger feasible choice sets do not
guarantee a better attained incumbent at a finite cutoff; changing screening
can also break feasible-set nesting.

Within the h300 block, all five exported decision vectors and objectives are
identical while time and memory differ. One thread is fastest and least
memory-intensive in this observed sequence. Fixed order, shared-node workload,
SMT, nonexclusive resources and one observation per level prevent causal speedup,
parallel-efficiency or universal thread-ranking claims. Large continuous
relaxations, memory traffic, presolve and degeneracy can matter even with few
integer nodes. The measurements do not identify proprietary internal algorithms.
The practical implication is to report the tested configuration and attainable
quality, rather than equating more allocated CPUs with more useful parallelism.

## Interpreting the matched solver campaign

The first common-Pyomo h300 pair establishes that both studied solvers can
return independently accepted plans for the same large agricultural instance.
Gurobi returned earlier with a smaller attained gap in this pair; HiGHS also
reached the prescribed quality within its allowance. The observed contrast
therefore concerns two successful implementations, their attained quality
and the resources they required. It does not support a general division
between problems that commercial and open-source software can solve.

The preliminary h300 terminal records in Appendix C extend the descriptive
comparison. All 13 Gurobi previews and the one-thread HiGHS preview record
accepted independent validation and gaps within 1%. Eight HiGHS previews
at higher thread ceilings reached the native time limit without an incumbent.
The preview set has unequal coverage across settings and awaits archive
collection. Its observed runtimes and censoring motivate separate reporting
of quality and effort by solver and thread ceiling.

Both completed h300 runs processed one integer node and reported several
million LP iterations. Those counters motivate examining root processing
and the continuous relaxation alongside integer search. They do not isolate
which phase caused the runtime difference. In particular, the version-specific
HiGHS parallel-search setting does not imply parallel simplex in MIP
relaxations. Additional configured threads may therefore have limited benefit
for some workloads. The forthcoming measurements test that possibility rather
than presupposing a speedup or a preferred thread count.

The study complements the tactical resource measurements of @reis2023
by linking computation to long-lived warehouse investments and
scenario-dependent flows. The discrete sizing and demand fulfillment of
@pourmohammadi2020 clarify how continuous sizing and penalized shortage
change the interpretation of a capacity plan. The overflow mechanism
examined by @milanez2026 provides a precedent for reporting capacity
relief alongside a numerical gap. Here the gap pertains to the penalized
objective, and the independent service and exceedance measures describe
its operational consequences. The computational comparison uses the
matched instances within this study.

## Penalty effects and agricultural interpretation

The three slack families enlarge only their encoded demand, static-stock and
reception constraints. Shipping, route eligibility, activation and conservation
remain hard. Positive slack is compatible with an accepted solution to this
model; it is not evidence that the corresponding physical network can operate
without additional measures. Nor does it prove that a no-slack model is
infeasible. A penalty magnitude cannot establish a monotonic runtime effect
or demonstrate that slack caused rapid convergence.

Artificial penalties account for approximately 94–97% of the reported scalar
totals. This concentration makes the global gap a certificate about the
penalized total, not a 1%-accurate economic subtotal or a service guarantee.
Investment/operating expenditure, artificial penalties and physical shortages
or exceedances therefore remain separately visible. The same coefficients and numerical validation criteria are used throughout
the reported cohort.

The W/D comparison makes this distinction concrete. Direct delivery can
bypass warehouse reception and storage, allowing the scalar objective to
balance lower capacity-related penalties against a different domestic-shortage
outcome. In the returned D plans, lower penalized costs coexist with more
unmet domestic demand. The model permits that trade-off because shortage and
capacity exceedance have explicit weights; it does not impose full domestic
service as a hard requirement. A decision-maker would therefore need to assess
the service and investment consequences jointly. Introducing a service floor
or recalibrating penalties would be a new model-policy study, rather than a
reinterpretation of the existing certificates.

All included candidates receive positive capacity in the accepted vectors.
The plans are consequently not sparse selections of a few hubs. Under the
frozen cost translation, available options and penalty trade-offs, adding
candidate locations broadens distributed investment and operating opportunities.
Existing-site expansion and bulkification provide additional, distinct choices.
The model's extensive investment and remaining slack identify limits of the
encoded planning system; they are not a ready-to-build public investment program.
Engineering suitability, finance, contracts, quality and governance remain
outside the mathematical abstraction.

Static exceedance summed over time is expressed in tonne-periods, not installed
tonnes. Reception overflow is tonnes within periods and can be divided by
operating days only for a derived daily equivalent. Transport-leg totals may
count the same grain through several arcs, so they are not unique production.
Scenario-weighted logistics aggregates and selected-scenario views answer
different questions. These distinctions prevent superficially attractive maps
or totals from overstating service improvements and infrastructure requirements.

For a planning organization, application time matters alongside native solver
time: model assembly, transfer, extraction and checking all precede a usable
decision report. In the first matched pair, these complete application times
are approximately 92 and 443 minutes. Such observations help assess whether
an available computational environment can support repeated strategic
analyses within the organization's planning cycle. They do not establish
real-time decision support, deployment costs or a universal software choice.

The two plans also illustrate why a small MIP gap is only one part of decision
support. Both open 154 candidates, but the expansion and bulk-handling lists
differ. Similar aggregate costs and service therefore need not identify one
unique investment program. Comparing the complete facility-ID lists can
reveal which recommendations change with the returned incumbent. That is
sensitivity to computational outcomes under fixed assumptions, rather than
demonstrated robustness to market, climate or demand uncertainty.

Expected unmet tonnes are weighted across the modeled horizon and scenarios;
they are not an observed annual national deficit. Likewise, modeled financial
subtotals are not validated construction bids or realized welfare changes.
The practical contribution is a traceable way to inspect investment options,
remaining service limitations and computational requirements together. Turning
those outputs into a project portfolio requires site and engineering review,
locally credible costs and an explicit assessment of the service trade-offs.

## Contribution to agricultural computing

The computational contribution lies in connecting strategic grain-network
structure to observed construction effort, memory requirements, attainable
quality and the interpretation of returned plans. It complements the location
and decision-support questions in @essien2018 and @gholamian2017 and the
uncertainty concerns in @hosseini2020 and @reis2023. Their existence rules out
a generic novelty claim based only on combining location and uncertainty.

The comparison with @shastri2011 is methodological: decomposition and distributed
optimization address computational burden through a solution strategy, whereas
this cohort examines a direct extensive-form implementation. Its times cannot
be ranked against theirs without a matched model, data, equipment and stopping
rule. Distributed simulation and spatial-processing studies likewise concern
different workloads. The present observations support a configuration-specific
assessment of attainable scale and resource use, with original feasibility and
bound information, rather than an algorithmic superiority claim.

C2 adds a related planning lesson. A quality-qualified penalized objective can
coexist with substantial shortages and capacity exceedances, and the
direct-enabled plans can reduce that objective while worsening domestic service.
This is useful information about the encoded trade-off, but it does not convert
uncalibrated artificial weights into observed economic damages or prove that
the plans are ready for implementation.

Integrated decision support requires connecting model outputs to their
operational and institutional meaning [@mardaneh2021]. The complementary
Human–AI account documents how scientific assumptions and computational
proposals were supervised and checked; it does not quantify productivity or
independently accredit the assistants. Appendix B retains that methodological
detail while the article's central claim remains the bounded computational
and agricultural assessment.

# Final considerations, limitations and future work

The eleven accepted scalar observations meet the declared 1% global-gap target:
h215 W DET/STO, five h300 W thread observations, h400/h500 W STO, and the
separate h215 D DET/STO pair. Together, they support empirical
computational characterization and an applied interpretation of the returned
plans, including substantial investment and residual permitted shortages.
Separate Pyomo/APPSI Gurobi and HiGHS h215 STO observations also pass
independent validation and the gap target. These observations do not establish
exact optimality, full service, a universal solver frontier or a causal thread
speedup.

At h500, the retained gap is 0.207432%, native runtime is 7654.77 seconds
and sampled application peak RSS is 111.78 GiB. Domestic service is 91.636%
and artificial penalties account for 94.074% of the scalar objective. All
354 included candidates receive positive capacity. These results support
bounded empirical feasibility and quality, not full service, economic-subtotal
precision or a causal population-size effect. Experiments using different objectives or stopping rules are excluded from
this scalar comparison.

Limitations include controlled rather than empirically fitted scenarios,
finite resource budgets, one observation per thread level, shared-node load,
incomplete physical cost calibration and unavailable road polylines in the
current geographic exports. The fixed penalties express the modeled trade-off,
not observed damages or a demonstrated service policy. Detailed source
identities and uncertainty about unobserved peaks constrain interpretation.

The completed Pyomo observations establish that both Gurobi and HiGHS can
return independently accepted h215 W STO plans under their declared profiles.
Their attained gaps differ: 0.740159% for Gurobi and 0.000196% for HiGHS.
Their native runtimes, 31.54 and 426.70 minutes, therefore cannot be interpreted
as time to an identical solution quality. The repeated common-Pyomo campaign
addresses a more controlled comparison across populations and thread counts.
Its first h300 pair is reported separately: Gurobi and HiGHS reached
0.004105% and 0.006879% gaps in 48.23 and 401.43 native minutes, respectively.
The common inputs and ordered algebra agree. This first descriptive pair
does not yet establish repeated-run variability or parallel efficiency.

Future work can examine repeated measurements under controlled resource
conditions, decomposition methods and sensitivity to the artificial
coefficients. Agricultural application also requires better calibration of
investment and operating costs, scrutiny of location suitability and explicit
service requirements. These extensions address the limits of the present
computational and planning evidence.

# Reproducibility and availability

The source code, experiment definitions and numerical records are available in
[Model Agrologistic](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/model-agrologistic).
Each experimental record identifies the source version, input, warehouse
population, settings, decisions and original validation. A later integrity
check does not change the identities of the executed software or its results.

The article and supplementary material are written in Quarto and can be
rendered without an optimizer or HPC credentials. Appendix A presents the
literature review; Appendix B explains AI-assisted research and verification;
Appendix C describes the Python implementations, independent validation and
GAMS translation; Appendix D specifies input data and effective parameters.
GAMS compilation and numerical parity have not been verified. The Python
results therefore do not constitute numerical validation of that translation.

The supplementary material is accessible as
[HTML](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/supplementary-review.html)
and [PDF](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/supplementary-review.pdf).
Exact source snapshots and data identities are given in the linked repository.

The editable [article TeX](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/index.tex)
and [appendix TeX](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/supplementary-review.tex)
are generated from the Quarto sources. Their figures, bibliography, class files
and notices accompany the [complete editable project](https://unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc.github.io/model-agrologistic/editable-sources.zip).
The individual TeX downloads are intended for editing; compilation requires
those accompanying dependencies.

## Data availability

The research dataset is publicly available in Zenodo, version 0.2.0
[@celestino2026dataset], at
[10.5281/zenodo.22751909](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22751909).
It contains selected historical inputs, population records, road audits
and evidence inventories. Appendices D and E identify the additional
source-bound workbooks, model inputs, decision vectors and flow-distance
companions and distinguish their access status. Distribution of external
inputs and derivatives depends on their file-level source and
redistribution terms. Additional research records awaiting rights or
access review are identified in the repository inventories. OpenStreetMap
derivatives retain ODbL terms, and project-authored code is MIT.
